title: Fitbit Charge 3 oxygen-variation signals precede COVID-19 exacerbation in 4 of 5 cases and reveal severe sleep apnoea in one patient (DEXTERITY pilot, Kanazawa)
summary: Kanazawa pilot, 23 COVID-19 patients (2020): Fitbit oxygen-variation signals preceded 4 of 5 exacerbations (sensitivity 80%); one man's persistent signals led to polysomnography showing severe OSAS.
account: Yamagami, Nomura and colleagues at Kanazawa University and the Japan Community Health Care Organization (JCHO) Kanazawa Hospital published the DEXTERITY pilot in JMIR Formative Research on 16 September 2021 (used as the date observed; the study ran from August to November 2020 and the individual event is undated). Twenty-three patients with PCR-confirmed COVID-19 wore a Fitbit Charge 3 for 30 days; the investigators defined a high 'estimated oxygen variation' (EOV) signal as a significant dip and recovery of the oxygen level within the index period and counted a prediction as successful if the signal appeared within two days before an exacerbation. Exacerbation occurred in six patients (seven events); EOV signals preceded four of five analyzed cases (sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%), better than resting-heart-rate signals (50% and 80%). Separately, patient JCHO-023, a 53-year-old man with hypertension who had recovered from COVID-19, showed 'a long-lasting high EOV signal' from days 18 to 29 without symptoms; the team suspected sleep apnoea, and a portable polysomnogram (Nihon Kohden SAS-2200) gave a 3% oxygen desaturation index of 33.6 per hour, severe obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome. The paper reports no treatment for him. The authors note that the Fitbit's functions and analysis algorithms were not approved as a medical device at the time, that baseline data were short, and that the five exacerbation cases are too few to generalize; the prediction analysis was defined against outcomes after the fact rather than as live alerts.
purpose: Fitbit's EOV metric summarizes overnight oxygen variation for consumers; the investigators repurposed it to flag COVID-19 deterioration, and the sleep-apnoea finding was incidental to that study aim.
system: Fitbit Charge 3 estimated oxygen variation (EOV) and resting heart rate, with investigator-defined signal thresholds
developer: Fitbit (device and EOV algorithm); Kanazawa University investigators (signal definitions)
deployer: Kanazawa University and JCHO Kanazawa Hospital (DEXTERITY pilot, UMIN000041421)
taxonomy_note: No health type exists; chosen because the device supplied information (overnight oxygen variation) that led to a diagnosis and, in aggregate, flagged deterioration. The aggregate prediction result is a retrospective pilot analysis, so only the sleep-apnoea case is an attributable event. The paper does not describe Fitbit's EOV algorithm as machine learning, so the AI character of the system rests on the device's undisclosed algorithm. Source is the independent investigators' peer-reviewed paper; no vendor source was used.

ratings.reason: One man received a diagnosis of severe obstructive sleep apnoea (3% ODI 33.6/h) from an incidental wearable signal; the paper reports no treatment or follow-up for him.
The 80% sensitivity for predicting exacerbation is a retrospective pilot result on five events, which the authors say is too small to generalize; no live alerting or changed care is documented.

ai_role.statement: The device produced the EOV values; the investigators' own rule flagged high signals and clinicians decided to order polysomnography for the sleep-apnoea patient. The paper does not say whether Fitbit's EOV estimation uses machine learning and notes the functions were not approved as a medical device; the COVID-19 prediction figures were computed after the outcomes were known, not from alerts acted on in real time.

produced_by: A Fitbit Charge 3 worn for 30 days by patients with PCR-confirmed COVID-19, with EOV and resting heart rate extracted
An investigator-defined high-EOV signal (a significant dip and recovery of the oxygen level within the index period) reviewed by the study team
Weekly phone calls to discharged patients and access to portable polysomnography
must_hold: Patients can pair the device with a smartphone app (elderly patients unable to use a smartphone were not enrolled)
Enough baseline data to separate abnormal signals from normal variation, which the authors list as lacking in the 30-day window
